meaningEnglish: The Ancient Lore of the Lord (bhāgavata = of/relating to Bhagavan, the Lord; purāṇa = ancient lore)
historicalContext: The Bhagavata Purana (also called Bhagavatam or Srimad Bhagavatam) is considered the most important of the Vaishnava Puranas. Traditionally attributed to Vyasa, it is composed between 800–1000 CE. It consists of 12 skandhas (books) and approximately 18,000 shlokas. Book 10 on Krishna's life is the most celebrated.
explanation: The Bhagavata Purana is the primary scripture of the bhakti movement and of Vaishnavism. Book 10 (the largest, with over 4,000 verses) narrates Krishna's life in Vrindavana with the gopis, his killing of Kamsa, and his later life. Book 11 contains the Uddhava Gita (sometimes called the 'eleventh Gita'). Book 2 contains the description of the Purusha form. The opening shloka 'dharmasya hyāpavargasya' is the foundational statement of its theology.

sanskritPassages.sanskrit: धर्मः प्रोज्झितकैतवोऽत्र परमो निर्मत्सराणां सतां वेद्यं वास्तवमत्र वस्तु शिवदं तापत्रयोन्मूलनम् ।
sanskritPassages.transliteration: dharmaḥ projjhitakaitavo'tra paramo nirmatsarāṇāṃ satāṃ vedyaṃ vāstavam atra vastu śivadaṃ tāpatrayonmūlanam
sanskritPassages.translation: Completely rejecting all religious activities which are materially motivated, this Bhagavat Purana propounds the highest truth, which is understandable by those devotees who are fully pure in heart.

historicalContext: The Vishnu Purana is one of the oldest Mahapuranas, estimated to have been composed between 1st–4th century CE. It consists of 6 books (amshas) and approximately 7,000 shlokas. It is classified as a sattvic Purana and is traditionally associated with the Paushkara recension.
explanation: The Vishnu Purana begins with a cosmogonic account of Brahman's creative activity, describes the nature and attributes of Vishnu, narrates the Samudra Manthan (churning of the ocean), tells the story of the Dhruva, Prahlada, and other devotees, and ends with descriptions of the Kali Yuga and the future Kalki avatar. Its account of Krishna's childhood (Book 5) is a major source for the Krishna legend.

historicalContext: The Shiva Purana is one of the principal Shaiva Mahapuranas, composed between 10th–14th century CE (with earlier cores). It consists of 7 Samhitas (sections) and approximately 24,000 shlokas. It is classified as a tamasic Purana by some traditional classifications.
explanation: The Shiva Purana narrates the greatness of Shiva, accounts of the twelve Jyotirlingas (sacred Shiva shrines), the significance of Shiva worship, the story of the destruction of Tripura (three demon cities), Shiva's marriage to Parvati, and accounts of his ganas and devotees. It is the central scriptural source for Shaiva devotional practice.

meaningEnglish: The Ancient Lore of the Goddess (devī = goddess; bhāgavata = of the Lord/Goddess)
historicalContext: The Devi Bhagavata Purana is the primary Shakta Mahapurana, consisting of 12 skandhas and approximately 18,000 shlokas. Composed between 7th–12th century CE. The Shakta tradition considers it a Mahapurana in the same category as the Bhagavata Purana. It is the central scripture of Shaktism.
explanation: The Devi Bhagavata Purana narrates the goddess's cosmic activities, her forms as Mahakali, Mahalakshmi, and Mahasaraswati, her battles against demons, the establishment of the Shakti Peethas (sacred sites where parts of Sati's body fell), and elaborate philosophical discussions on the nature of Shakti as supreme Brahman.

historicalContext: The Brahma Purana is listed first among the 18 Mahapuranas in traditional enumerations. It consists of approximately 10,000 shlokas. It is associated with the Brahma tradition and contains information about the Jagannath temple at Puri, Odisha.
explanation: The Brahma Purana covers the cosmogonic accounts including the story of the solar dynasty (Suryavamsha), the genealogies of the sages, accounts of pilgrimage sites (particularly along the Godavari river), and descriptions of Vishnu's avatars. It provides detailed accounts of the Jagannath cult at Purushottama Kshetra (Puri).

meaningEnglish: The Ancient Lore of Markandeya (the sage Markandeya, known for his great age and devotion to Shiva)
historicalContext: The Markandeya Purana consists of approximately 9,000 shlokas and is attributed to the sage Markandeya, narrating to Jaimini. It is one of the older Mahapuranas, estimated to have been composed between 300–600 CE. It contains the Devi Mahatmya (also called Chandi or Durga Saptashati) in chapters 81–93.
explanation: The Markandeya Purana is best known for the Devi Mahatmya — 700 verses celebrating the goddess Durga's battles against the demons Madhu-Kaitabha, Mahishasura, and Shumbha-Nishumbha. The Devi Mahatmya is the most important Shakta text in terms of liturgical use and is recited during Navratri. The Purana also contains accounts of cosmology, dynasties, and the ages of the world.

meaningEnglish: The Ancient Lore of Skanda (Kartikeya/Murugan, son of Shiva)
historicalContext: The Skanda Purana is the largest of the 18 Mahapuranas, consisting of approximately 81,000 shlokas. It is composed between 7th–12th century CE and exists in various regional recensions. It is named after Skanda (Kartikeya/Murugan) and contains extensive mahatmya (glorification) literature for pilgrimage sites across India.
explanation: The Skanda Purana consists of seven Khandas (sections), each covering different regions and their sacred sites. It is the primary source of mahatmya literature for many Hindu pilgrimage sites, including Varanasi (Kashi), Badrinath, and numerous South Indian temples. Its account of Skanda's birth and his wars against Tarakasura are found in the Shankara Samhita.

meaningEnglish: The Ancient Lore of Fire (Agni narrates it; an encyclopedic Purana covering multiple subjects)
historicalContext: The Agni Purana consists of approximately 15,000 shlokas and is narrated by Agni to the sage Vasishtha. Composed between 8th–12th century CE, it is an encyclopedic text covering a vast range of subjects from cosmogony and temple rituals to poetics, medicine, and military science.
explanation: The Agni Purana is unique for its encyclopedic scope: it covers avatars of Vishnu, cosmology, temple construction (shilpa shastra), ayurveda, military science, astronomy, grammar, poetics (including the theory of dhvani/suggestion), law, and geography. It contains one of the early treatments of Sanskrit poetics, making it important for Indian literary theory as well.

meaningEnglish: The Ancient Lore of Garuda (the eagle-vehicle of Vishnu who narrates the text)
historicalContext: The Garuda Purana is narrated by Vishnu to his vehicle Garuda. Composed between 800–1000 CE, it consists of approximately 19,000 shlokas. It is traditionally recited after a person's death as a means of guiding the departed soul, and is associated with the rites for the dead (Pitru Paksha).
explanation: The Garuda Purana covers cosmology, descriptions of hell and heaven, the journey of the soul after death, rites for the dead (antyeshti and shraddha), Ayurveda, and devotional practices. Its Preta Khanda (section on the dead) is extensively used in Hindu funeral rites and contains detailed accounts of the soul's journey, the nature of karmic judgment, and descriptions of various hells and their nature.

sources.text: Garuda Purana, Preta Khanda 1.1 (soul after death)

meaningEnglish: The Ancient Lore of the Lotus (padma = lotus; the Purana associated with Brahma's emergence from the lotus and with Vishnu/Lakshmi)
historicalContext: The Padma Purana is one of the largest Mahapuranas, consisting of approximately 55,000 shlokas in five sections (khandas): Srishti Khanda (creation), Bhumi Khanda (earth), Svarga Khanda (heaven), Patala Khanda (netherworld), and Uttara Khanda. It is a strongly Vaishnava text and is classified as a sattvic Purana. It contains the influential Bhagavata Mahatmya, which glorifies the Bhagavata Purana.
explanation: The Padma Purana covers Vishnu's cosmic activities, the glory of Vishnu worship, accounts of sacred tirthas (pilgrimage sites), detailed descriptions of vrata (religious observances), and extensive Vaishnava theology. The Uttara Khanda contains the Ramayana narrative as told by Shiva to Parvati (Parvati Ramayan). The text is an important source for understanding the spread of Vaishnava practice and pilgrimage culture across India.

meaningEnglish: The Ancient Lore of Vayu (vāyu = wind, the wind god; narrated by the wind god Vayu)
historicalContext: The Vayu Purana is one of the oldest of the Mahapuranas, with a core estimated to date as early as 200–400 CE, making it among the earliest datable Puranic texts. It consists of approximately 24,000 shlokas. It has a Shaiva orientation and is an important source for early Hindu chronology, genealogy of royal dynasties, and cosmology. Some traditions consider the Vayu and Shiva Puranas as closely related recensions.
explanation: The Vayu Purana covers cosmogony, the system of cosmic ages (yugas and kalpas), genealogies of the solar and lunar dynasties, accounts of the Saptarishis (seven sages), descriptions of Shiva and Shaiva practice, and geography of the sacred world. Its account of dynastic genealogies is an important resource for reconstructing ancient Indian history. It contains one of the earliest versions of the Puranic cosmological system in systematic form.

meaningEnglish: The Ancient Lore of the Linga (liṅga = mark, sign; the iconic form of Shiva as a cylindrical form representing formless divinity)
historicalContext: The Linga Purana consists of approximately 11,000 shlokas in two parts (purva and uttara bhaga). Composed between 5th–10th century CE. It is primarily a Shaiva text explaining the significance of the Linga form of Shiva worship and narrating Shiva's cosmic activities.
explanation: The Linga Purana explains the origin and significance of Shiva worship through the Linga, which represents the formless, infinite, divine reality. It narrates the story of the Jyotirlinga — the pillar of light that appeared between Brahma and Vishnu and from which the twelve sacred Jyotirlingas derive. It covers Shaiva cosmology, descriptions of Shiva's manifestations, and the greatness of Shiva devotion.
